claim: The Tara Oceans project produced a total of 24.2 terabases of metagenomic sequence reads.
source: The Tara Oceans project produced a total of 24.2 terabases of metagenomic sequence reads (Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the total amount of metagenomic sequence data produced, with reference to a supplementary table.

claim: DNA sequence data was obtained from samples collected at 113 worldwide stations during the Tara Oceans expedition.
source: DNA sequence data was obtained from samples collected at 113 worldwide stations during the Tara Oceans expedition.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of sampling stations.

claim: Each plankton community sample was sequenced for up to six operational size fractions: one virus-enriched (0–0.22 μm; Roux et al., 2016), one prokaryote-enriched (either 0.22–1.6 or 0.22–3 μm; Sunagawa et al., 2015), and four eukaryote-enriched (0.8–5 μm, 5–20 μm, 20–180 μm, and 180–2000 μm; de Vargas et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
source: Each plankton community sample was sequenced for up to six operational size fractions: one virus-enriched (0–0.22 μm; Roux et al., 2016), one prokaryote-enriched (either 0.22–1.6 or 0.22–3 μm; Sunagawa et al., 2015), and four eukaryote-enriched (0.8–5 μm, 5–20 μm, 20–180 μm, and 180–2000 μm; de Vargas et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the size fractions used for sequencing with supporting citations and references to a figure.

claim: The average percentage of metagenomic sequence reads in samples from the prokaryote-enriched 0.22–1.6/3 µm size fractions that were of eukaryotic origin was estimated to be 12%.
source: We estimated the average percentage of metagenomic sequence reads in samples from the prokaryote-enriched 0.22–1.6/3 µm size fractions that were of eukaryotic origin to be 12%
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative estimate based on analysis of the data.

claim: The average percentage of reads in eukaryote-enriched size fractions that were of prokaryote origin was: 0.8–5 μm: 39%, 5–20 μm: 23%, 20–180 μm: 3%, 180–2000 μm: 5%.
source: the average percentage of reads in eukaryote-enriched size fractions that were of prokaryote origin as follows: 0.8–5 μm: 39%, 5–20 μm: 23%, 20–180 μm: 3%, 180–2000 μm: 5% (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative estimates for each size fraction.

claim: Metagenomic and OTU dissimilarities were correlated for all size fractions (Spearman's ρ 0.53–0.97, p≤10−4, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
source: Metagenomic and OTU dissimilarities were correlated for all size fractions (Spearman's ρ 0.53–0.97, p≤10−4, Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values with statistical significance and references a figure.

claim: Substantial metagenomic dissimilarities (average pairwise dissimilarity >80%) were observed between sampled stations across all size fractions.
source: Globally, we observed substantial metagenomic dissimilarities (average pairwise dissimilarity >80%) between sampled stations (including adjacent sites) across all size fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a, Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the observed dissimilarity values with reference to a figure.

claim: Robust evidence exists for the existence of large-scale biogeographical patterns within all plankton size classes.
source: Overlying this heterogeneity, we found robust evidence for the existence of large-scale biogeographical patterns within all plankton size classes using two complementary analyses of dissimilarity among samples (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-f, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Appendix 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states finding robust evidence with references to multiple figures and an appendix.

claim: Genomic provinces were mostly composed of geographically clustered stations.
source: Genomic provinces were mostly composed of geographically clustered stations (consistent with previous studies documenting patterns in plankton biogeography [Hanson et al., 2012; Martiny et al., 2006; McGowan and Walker, 1979; Roux et al., 2016; Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-f]).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the geographic clustering with supporting citations and figure references.

claim: Genomic provinces of smaller plankton (viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotes <20 µm) tended to be limited to a single ocean basin.
source: Genomic provinces of smaller plankton (viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotes <20 µm), with some exceptions (e.g. genomic province B5), tended to be limited to a single ocean basin and to approximately correspond to Longhurst biogeochemical provinces (BGCPs; Longhurst, 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-d; Appendix 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the geographic extent of genomic provinces for smaller plankton with citations and figure references.

claim: Provinces of larger plankton (micro- and mesoplankton, >20 µm) spanned multiple basins.
source: In contrast, provinces of larger plankton (micro- and mesoplankton, >20 µm) spanned multiple basins (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e-f, Appendix 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts the geographic extent of larger plankton provinces with figure references.

claim: Seawater surface temperature was significantly different among genomic provinces for all plankton size classes (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<10−5).
source: Seawater surface temperature was significantly different among genomic provinces for all plankton size classes (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<10−5)
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific statistical test result showing significant differences.

claim: For all plankton size classes, community composition differences between stations were significantly correlated to travel time.
source: For all plankton size classes, community composition differences between stations were significantly correlated to travel time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correlation with reference to a figure.

claim: Cumulative correlation values were maximal for pairs of stations separated by Tmin <~1.5 years for all size classes, with correlation values (Spearman's ρ 0.45–0.71 depending on size class, p≤10–4; Figure 2a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
source: Cumulative correlation values were maximal for pairs of stations separated by Tmin <~1.5 years for all size classes, with correlation values (Spearman's ρ 0.45–0.71 depending on size class, p≤10–4; Figure 2a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values with statistical significance and figure references.

claim: β-diversity calculated from zooplankton imaging was correlated with metagenomic dissimilarity (Spearman's ρ between 0.32 and 0.60; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
source: β-diversity calculated from zooplankton imaging was correlated with metagenomic dissimilarity (Spearman's ρ between 0.32 and 0.60; Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values with reference to a figure.

claim: Metagenomic and MAG β-diversity were highly correlated (Spearman's ρ 0.94).
source: Metagenomic and MAG β-diversity were highly correlated (Spearman's ρ 0.94)
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific correlation value.

claim: Differences in environmental conditions for pairs of stations covaried with transit time for Tmin <~1.5 years.
source: Differences in environmental conditions for pairs of stations also covaried (although less strongly) with transit time for Tmin <~1.5 years (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the covariation with reference to a figure.

claim: Beyond ~1.5 years of transport, correlations of Tmin with metagenomic dissimilarity decreased.
source: In our data, beyond ~1.5 years of transport, correlations of Tmin with metagenomic dissimilarity decreased (Figures 2a and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-e)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the decrease in correlations with figure references.

claim: Temperature remained well correlated for longer transit times while the correlation between Tmin and nutrient concentrations decreased.
source: A similar trend was observed for the correlation between Tmin and nutrient concentrations, whereas temperature, the gradients of which are mostly dictated by Earth-scale processes that are unaffected by plankton communities, remained well correlated for longer transit times (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts the behavior of temperature and nutrient correlations with reference to a figure.

claim: The smaller size classes (<20 µm) had a shorter metagenomic turnover time (ca. 1 year) than larger plankton (ca. 2 years; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Appendix 6).
source: In the case of the North Atlantic current system (including the Mediterranean Sea), a simple exponential fit of metagenomic dissimilarity along Tmin for Tmin <~1.5 years (Figure 2c) revealed that the smaller size classes (<20 µm) had a shorter metagenomic turnover time (ca. 1 year) than larger plankton (ca. 2 years; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Appendix 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific turnover times derived from exponential fits with figure references.

claim: Genomic provinces of small size classes corresponded with differences in environmental parameters such as nutrient levels.
source: At global geographical scales, the genomic provinces of small size classes, which are enriched in phytoplankton (de Vargas et al., 2015; Frémont et al., 2022; Sommeria-Klein et al., 2021; Sunagawa et al., 2015), corresponded in our data with differences in environmental parameters such as nutrient levels (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 7)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correspondence with supporting citations and figure references.

claim: Genomic provinces of larger plankton were more related to global scale gradients and circulation patterns, notably major latitudinal temperature zones or the separation between Atlantic and Indo-Pacific large-scale surface circulations.
source: On the other hand, genomic provinces of larger plankton, enriched in heterotrophic and symbiotic organisms (de Vargas et al., 2015; Frémont et al., 2022; Sommeria-Klein et al., 2021), were less coupled with geochemical parameters and were more related to global scale gradients and circulation patterns, notably major latitudinal temperature zones (Martin et al., 2021) or the separation between Atlantic and Indo-Pacific large-scale surface circulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e,f,i).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the relationship with supporting citations and figure references.

claim: For smaller plankton, correlations with differences in nutrient concentrations were strongest at Tmin up to ~1.5 years.
source: For smaller plankton, correlations with differences in nutrient concentrations were strongest, at Tmin up to ~1.5 years, while for larger plankton, correlations were strongest with temperature variations, for Tmin beyond ~1.5 years.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts the correlation patterns for different plankton sizes.

claim: For larger plankton, correlations were strongest with temperature variations for Tmin beyond ~1.5 years.
source: For smaller plankton, correlations with differences in nutrient concentrations were strongest, at Tmin up to ~1.5 years, while for larger plankton, correlations were strongest with temperature variations, for Tmin beyond ~1.5 years.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts the correlation patterns for different plankton sizes.

claim: The use of DNA as a primary proxy for global plankton diversity has several important advantages over classical morphology-based analyses.
source: The use of DNA as a primary proxy for global plankton diversity has several important advantages over classical morphology-based analyses, notably because methods can be standardized and applied across the entire range of plankton sizes, from viruses through prokaryotes and protists to animals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the advantages of DNA-based methods.

claim: Plankton communities are constantly on the move, transported by ocean currents.
source: Plankton communities are constantly on the move, transported by ocean currents.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this fundamental characteristic of plankton.

claim: Transport involves both advection and mixing.
source: Transport involves both advection and mixing.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the components of transport.

claim: While being advected by currents, plankton can be influenced by multiple processes, both physicochemical (fluxes of heat, light,and nutrients Moore et al., 2013) and biological (species interactions, life cycles, behavior, and acclimation/adaptation [Armbrust, 2009; Flynn et al., 2015]).
source: While being advected by currents, plankton can be influenced by multiple processes, both physicochemical (fluxes of heat, light,and nutrients Moore et al., 2013) and biological (species interactions, life cycles, behavior, and acclimation/adaptation [Armbrust, 2009; Flynn et al., 2015])

claim: Plankton impact seawater physicochemistry while they are being advected (Moore et al., 2013).
source: In turn, plankton impact seawater physicochemistry while they are being advected (Moore et al., 2013).

claim: The community composition and biogeochemical properties of a water mass at a given site are partially dependent on its history of mixing with neighboring water masses during transport.
source: The community composition and biogeochemical properties of a water mass at a given site are also partially dependent on its history of mixing with neighboring water masses during transport.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship.

claim: Previous studies on plankton distribution have tended to be geographically or taxonomically restricted (Hanson et al., 2012; Martiny et al., 2006; McGowan and Walker, 1979; Reygondeau and Dunn, 2019; Roux et al., 2016).
source: Due to logistical and analytical constraints, previous studies on plankton distribution have tended to be geographically or taxonomically restricted (Hanson et al., 2012; Martiny et al., 2006; McGowan and Walker, 1979; Reygondeau and Dunn, 2019; Roux et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly characterizes previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: The Tara Oceans sampling largely focused on open ocean sites located in the main gyres.
source: Our sampling largely focused on open ocean sites located in the main gyres, but also included other areas with distinct oceanographic features, such as coastal upwelling zones and lagoons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sampling strategy with reference to a figure.

claim: The Tara Oceans sampling included areas with distinct oceanographic features, such as coastal upwelling zones and lagoons.
source: Our sampling largely focused on open ocean sites located in the main gyres, but also included other areas with distinct oceanographic features, such as coastal upwelling zones and lagoons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sampling strategy with reference to a figure.

claim: The analyses focus on the sunlit (epipelagic) layer of the ocean (subsurface and deep chlorophyll maximum [DCM] samples).
source: Our analyses focus on the sunlit (epipelagic) layer of the ocean (subsurface and deep chlorophyll maximum [DCM] samples)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the depth focus of the analyses.

claim: At lower depths (the mesopelagic and below), the relationship between plankton community composition and ocean transport may be different than at the surface.
source: at lower depths (the mesopelagic and below), the relationship between plankton community composition and ocean transport may be different than at the surface.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly speculates about deeper ocean dynamics.

claim: A subset of 11.9 terabases was analyzed after testing that this subset accurately represented the complete data set.
source: To account for uneven sequencing depth among samples, we analyzed a subset of 11.9 terabases, after testing that this subset accurately represented the complete data set (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the data subset used with justification.

claim: The study analyzed 738 million 18S V9 ribosomal DNA marker sequences in the eukaryote-enriched size fractions.
source: We also analyzed operational taxonomic units (OTUs, representing groups of genetically related organisms), consisting of previously published viral populations (Brum et al., 2015) previously derived bacterial 16S miTAGs (Sunagawa et al., 2015), and 738 million 18S V9 ribosomal DNA marker sequences in the eukaryote-enriched size fractions, enlarging a previously described Tara Oceans data set (de Vargas et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of sequences analyzed with supporting citations.

claim: Metagenomic dissimilarity highlighted differences in the genomic identity of organisms between stations at species and subspecies resolution.
source: Metagenomic dissimilarity highlighted, at species and subspecies resolution, differences in the genomic identity of organisms between stations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes what metagenomic dissimilarity measures.

claim: Pairwise metagenomic dissimilarities likely represent an overestimate of β-diversity.
source: Our metagenomic sampling resulted in pairwise metagenomic dissimilarities that likely represent an overestimate of β-diversity (Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges this limitation with reference to an appendix.

claim: An identical procedure was applied to compute metagenomic dissimilarity for all size fractions.
source: However, we applied an identical procedure to compute metagenomic dissimilarity for all size fractions (correlations among fractions ranged Spearman's ρ 0.6–0.9, p≤10−4, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the methodological consistency with correlation values and figure reference.

claim: OTU dissimilarity incorporated more numerous rare taxa within the plankton, but at genus or higher-level taxonomic resolution.
source: The more thoroughly sampled OTU dissimilarity, in contrast, incorporated more numerous rare taxa within the plankton, but at genus or higher-level taxonomic resolution (de Vargas et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts OTU dissimilarity with metagenomic dissimilarity with a supporting citation.

claim: Metagenomic and OTU dissimilarities provided coherent and complementary estimates of β-diversity.
source: Metagenomic and OTU dissimilarities were correlated for all size fractions (Spearman's ρ 0.53–0.97, p≤10−4, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that both proxies, although characterized by different sampling levels and taxonomic resolution, provided coherent and complementary estimates of β-diversity (Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the coherence of the two measures with correlation values and figure reference.

claim: The oceanic ecosystem is dominated by a small number of abundant and cosmopolitan taxa, with a much larger number of less abundant taxa found at fewer sampling sites.
source: The resulting portrait is of a heterogeneous oceanic ecosystem at all scales separating Tara Oceans sampling sites (even those separated by only a few kilometers), dominated by a small number of abundant and cosmopolitan taxa, with a much larger number of less abundant taxa found at fewer sampling sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b-e), corroborating other studies (de Vargas et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the abundance distribution with figure reference and supporting citation.

claim: Samples located in physically distant zones but with shared environmental conditions, such as oceanic upwellings, grouped together.
source: Although the large majority of our samples were located in oceanic gyres, samples located in physically distant zones but with shared environmental conditions, such as oceanic upwellings, also grouped together (e.g. genomic province B6 in the bacterial-enriched size fraction).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this grouping pattern with a specific example.

claim: The geography of combined nutrient and temperature variations resembled the biogeography of smaller plankton size classes.
source: The geography of combined nutrient and temperature variations resembled the biogeography of smaller plankton size classes (Figure 1a–b, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-d,h)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this resemblance with figure references.

claim: Temperature alone more closely matched the distribution of larger plankton.
source: whereas temperature alone more closely matched the distribution of larger plankton (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e,f,i), potentially reflecting different ecological constraints.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this match with figure references and offers an interpretation.

claim: Many genomic provinces were spatially consistent with ocean basin-scale circulation patterns.
source: Plankton biogeographical patterns suggested a particular role for large-scale surface transport (a core component of the seascape) in the emergence of spatial patterns of plankton community composition (as previously proposed [Clayton et al., 2013]), as many genomic provinces were spatially consistent with ocean basin-scale circulation patterns (such as western boundary currents or major subtropical gyres [Talley et al., 2011; Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-f]).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this consistency with supporting citations and figure references.

claim: The minimum travel time (Tmin) between pairs of Tara stations was used to infer the characteristic timescale of main transport paths.
source: We inferred the characteristic timescale of main transport paths between stations from trajectories computed with the physically well-constrained MITgcm ocean model (see Materials and methods), which takes into account directionalities (Watson et al., 2010) and meso- to large-scale circulation, potential dispersal barriers, and mixing effects (Goetze et al., 2017; Mousing et al., 2016). For this we used the minimum travel time (Jönsson and Watson, 2016; Tmin) between pairs of Tara stations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the method with supporting citations.

claim: The trajectories corresponded to the dominant paths that transport the majority of water volume and its contents (e.g. heat, nutrients, and plankton).
source: These trajectories corresponded to the dominant paths that transport the majority of water volume and its contents (e.g. heat, nutrients, and plankton; Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes what the trajectories represent with a figure reference.

claim: High correlations between metagenomic dissimilarity and Tmin for travel times up to 1.5 years correspond well with the average time to travel across a basin or gyre.
source: These high correlations between metagenomic dissimilarity and Tmin for travel times up to 1.5 years, which correspond well with the average time to travel across a basin or gyre (Lumpkin and Johnson, 2013), hence reveal measurable plankton community dynamics on time scales far longer than typical plankton growth rates or life cycles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correspondence with a supporting citation.

claim: No unimodal pattern was found for correlations between metagenomic dissimilarity and geographic distance.
source: In contrast, no such unimodal pattern was found for correlations between metagenomic dissimilarity and geographic distance (without traversing land; Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts the pattern with geographic distance with a figure reference.

claim: The existence of a size-class-dependent structure of plankton geography indicates that the continua vary among size fractions because of different reactions of organisms within the seascape.
source: The existence of a size-class-dependent (smaller or larger than 20 µm) structure of plankton geography indicates that the continua that we observe vary among size fractions because of different reactions of organisms within the seascape (i.e. the interplay among organismal biology, nutrients, and local environmental conditions), in agreement with a parallel survey based on taxonomic groups (Sommeria-Klein et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the size-dependent structure with a supporting citation.

claim: Correlations with ocean transport time were far weaker for zooplankton imaging data than for metagenomic data from all organismal size fractions.
source: However, correlations with ocean transport time were far weaker for zooplankton imaging data than for metagenomic data from all organismal size fractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the correlations with a figure reference.

claim: The weaker correlations for imaging data are interpreted as being a result of the expected significantly lower resolution in imaging data as compared to metagenomic data.
source: We interpret this as being a result of the expected significantly lower resolution in imaging data as compared to metagenomic data (a similar difference of resolution in OTU data versus metagenomic data is discussed in Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides an interpretation with reference to an appendix.

claim: 18.4% of metagenomic reads from the 20–180 µm size fraction were mapped to MAGs.
source: Finally, we also confirmed our metagenome sequence read comparison-based results by comparing them to β-diversity among sampling sites using a collection of MAGs, which are likely to represent the most abundant genomes, from the 20–180 µm size fraction (the size fraction in which the largest proportion of metagenomic reads were mapped to MAGs, 18.4%; Delmont et al., 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the percentage with a supporting citation.

claim: Metagenomic and MAG β-diversity displayed similar biogeographical patterns.
source: Metagenomic and MAG β-diversity were highly correlated (Spearman's ρ 0.94) and consequently they displayed similar biogeographical patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e,g).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the similarity with correlation value and figure references.

claim: The fact that simulated transport times and metagenomic dissimilarity were correlated despite a 3-year pan-season sampling campaign suggests that a large-scale impact of the seascape promotes the existence of a biogeographical structure that is resilient to seasonal or other smaller spatiotemporal variations.
source: The fact that simulated transport times and metagenomic dissimilarity were correlated despite a 3-year pan-season sampling campaign, which could be considered to weaken our inference, suggests instead that a large-scale impact of the seascape promotes the existence of a biogeographical structure at a large spatial scale that is resilient to seasonal or other smaller spatiotemporal variations
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the correlation in the context of the sampling design.

claim: Genomic provinces consist of stations sampled over an average of 4.7±2.8 different months and 2.7±1.2 different seasons.
source: (across all size fractions, genomic provinces consist of stations sampled over an average of 4.7±2.8 different months and 2.7±1.2 different seasons, adjusted for hemisphere).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides quantitative data on sampling temporal distribution.

claim: Seasonal variations have previously been shown to have minor effects on the boundary positions of BGCPs based on satellite data.
source: Consistent with our results, seasonal variations have previously been shown to have minor effects on the boundary positions of BGCPs based on satellite data, but not enough to affect the overall pattern of ocean regionalization (Reygondeau et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work supporting the resilience to seasonal variation.

claim: Changes in environmental conditions and plankton community composition are concurrent along large-scale oceanic current systems.
source: This indicates that changes in environmental conditions and plankton community composition are concurrent along large-scale oceanic current systems.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this concurrence based on the covariation analysis.

claim: Beyond ~1.5 years, the correlation of metagenomic dissimilarity with differences in temperature increased while that with differences in nutrients decreased.
source: Moreover, beyond ~1.5 years, the correlation of metagenomic dissimilarity with differences in temperature increased while that with differences in nutrients decreased (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-e)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the divergent correlation trends with figure references.

claim: Both correlations with metagenomic dissimilarity (temperature and nutrients) remained strong on time scales beyond ~1.5 years.
source: although both of these correlations with metagenomic dissimilarity remained strong on these time scales.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly notes the continued strength of correlations.

claim: Distant Tara Oceans stations experiencing similar oceanographic phenomena (notably temperature), e.g., upwelling zones, produce generally similar environmental conditions.
source: This might be related to distant Tara Oceans stations experiencing similar oceanographic phenomena (notably temperature), e.g., upwelling zones (stations 67, 92, and 135; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), producing generally similar environmental conditions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly offers this interpretation with specific examples and figure reference.

claim: The relatively large separation among sampling stations allowed detection of the large-scale effects of ocean circulation, which are superimposed on smaller-scale effects such as local patchiness and seasonality.
source: The relatively large separation (in terms of transport time and season) among sampling stations allowed us to detect the large-scale effects of ocean circulation, which are superimposed on smaller-scale effects such as local patchiness and seasonality (as previously observed Longhurst, 2006; Reygondeau et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly explains how the sampling design enabled detection of large-scale effects with supporting citations.

claim: Within ocean basins, smooth variations have emerged due to the periodic recirculation of within-basin currents.
source: Within ocean basins, as the intertwined dynamics of plankton and chemistry continuously occur along transport, smooth variations have emerged due to the periodic recirculation of within-basin currents.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this mechanism.

claim: Smooth variations in community structure and nutrient concentrations lead to stable, continuous patterns of changes.
source: This leads to stable, continuous patterns of changes in community structure and nutrient concentrations, and also explains how temporally stable genomic provinces can exist in the face of ocean currents.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this as an explanation.

claim: Higher heterogeneity in environmental conditions across different circulation patterns can disrupt the equilibrium of seascape processes within a given continuum, leading to a global delimitation into distinguishable ecological continua among different large-scale current systems.
source: Among ocean basins, depending on the sensitivity to the environment of a plankton community, higher heterogeneity in environmental conditions across different circulation patterns can disrupt the equilibrium of seascape processes within a given continuum, leading to a global delimitation into distinguishable ecological continua among different large-scale current systems, resulting in the genomic provinces that we detected.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this mechanism for inter-basin differences.

claim: Larger plankton are dominated by eukaryotes, often multicellular, with much longer life cycles, potentially leading to slower community turnover.
source: Larger plankton are dominated by eukaryotes, often multicellular, with much longer life cycles, potentially leading to slower community turnover.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes characteristics of larger plankton and their potential consequences.

claim: Organisms with long life cycles can be transported through basins spanning multiple biogeochemical niches in which they may encounter strong environmental variability.
source: Organisms with long life cycles, on the order of several months or years, can be transported through basins spanning multiple biogeochemical niches in which they may encounter strong environmental variability
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this consequence of long life cycles.

claim: The biogeography of larger plankton is less affected by nutrient limitation and rather depends on large-scale temperature gradients among basins.
source: As observed here, their biogeography is less affected by nutrient limitation and rather depends on large-scale temperature gradients among basins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation.

claim: The dependence on temperature may be linked to the known correlation between body size and organismal metabolic rate (Ikeda, 1985).
source: This dependence may be linked to the known correlation between body size and organismal metabolic rate (Ikeda, 1985).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this link with a supporting citation.

claim: Variants within populations of organisms with short life cycles have the capacity to increase their relative abundance within restricted ecological niches to which they are adapted.
source: Conversely, variants within populations of organisms with short life cycles have the capacity to increase their relative abundance within restricted ecological niches to which they are adapted.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly contrasts short-lived organisms with long-lived ones.

claim: The difference in biogeography between short-lived and long-lived organisms, detectable at genomic resolution, may not be picked up in analyses performed using biological traits with less resolution.
source: This difference, detectable at genomic resolution, may not be picked up in analyses performed using biological traits with less resolution.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly notes the importance of genomic resolution.

claim: The results indicate a significant size-based decoupling within planktonic food webs.
source: These results indicate a significant size-based decoupling within planktonic food webs.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Large size predators will encounter different prey when transiting through the genomic provinces of small sized organisms.
source: For example, large size predators will encounter different prey when transiting through the genomic provinces of small sized organisms (see Appendix 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides this example with reference to an appendix.

claim: The integration of seascape physical, chemical, and biological processes over time and space produces a quasi-stationary biological partitioning of the oceans that supersedes short-term variability and seasonal cycles.
source: Using analysis of standardized metagenomic data together with environmental and physical data, we reveal that, in a background of significant local patchiness, the integration of seascape physical, chemical, and biological processes over time and space produces a quasi-stationary biological partitioning of the oceans that supersedes short-term variability and seasonal cycles, ultimately generating global biogeographical patterns.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as a key finding.

claim: Transport by ocean currents acts essentially as a conveyor on which interacting environmental and biological effects are layered.
source: Although the strong cross-coupling among our metagenomic, environmental, and physical data prevents a systematic disentangling of their various influences, we hypothesize that transport by ocean currents acts essentially as a conveyor on which interacting environmental and biological effects are layered.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this hypothesis.

claim: Direct effects of currents (such as turbulent diffusivity) on plankton composition are hypothesized to be secondary.
source: In this hypothesis, direct effects of currents (such as turbulent diffusivity) on plankton composition are secondary, and instead environmental and biological effects occurring during transport result in the emergence of a global plankton biogeography in the surface ocean.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as part of the hypothesis.

claim: Environmental and biological effects occurring during transport result in the emergence of a global plankton biogeography in the surface ocean.
source: In this hypothesis, direct effects of currents (such as turbulent diffusivity) on plankton composition are secondary, and instead environmental and biological effects occurring during transport result in the emergence of a global plankton biogeography in the surface ocean.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as part of the hypothesis.

claim: The metagenomic data and simulations were limited to the sunlit layer of the ocean.
source: The ocean is a three-dimensional system in which the primary axis of variation is depth. Our metagenomic data and simulations were limited to the sunlit layer of the ocean and therefore capture one part of seascape dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

claim: Studies of the dynamics of plankton communities must consider the critical influence of ocean currents in stretching the distribution of both planktonic organisms and the physicochemical nature of the water mass in which they reside on the scale of basins.
source: Overall, our work shows that studies of the dynamics of plankton communities must consider the critical influence of ocean currents in stretching, on the scale of basins, the distribution of both planktonic organisms and the physicochemical nature of the water mass in which they reside.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as a key conclusion.

claim: The combination of ocean circulation modeling with the use of metagenomic DNA as a tracer of plankton communities provides a resolution above the minimum necessary for assessing the role of transport in community turnover over time and space.
source: We also demonstrate that the combination of ocean circulation modeling with the use of metagenomic DNA as a tracer of plankton communities provides a resolution above the minimum necessary for assessing the role of transport in community turnover over time and space.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this methodological conclusion.

claim: The open ocean planktonic ecosystem is fundamentally different in many ways from other major planetary ecosystems.
source: The open ocean planktonic ecosystem is fundamentally different in many ways from other major planetary ecosystems, and this study provides a basis to understand and potentially predict the structuring of the ocean ecosystem in a scenario of rapid environmental and current system changes (Beaugrand et al., 2002; Caesar et al., 2018; Frémont et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with supporting citations.

claim: This study provides a basis to understand and potentially predict the structuring of the ocean ecosystem in a scenario of rapid environmental and current system changes.
source: The open ocean planktonic ecosystem is fundamentally different in many ways from other major planetary ecosystems, and this study provides a basis to understand and potentially predict the structuring of the ocean ecosystem in a scenario of rapid environmental and current system changes (Beaugrand et al., 2002; Caesar et al., 2018; Frémont et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as a potential application with supporting citations.

claim: K-mers of 31 base pairs derived from the first 100 million reads sequenced in each sample were used to compute a similarity measure between all pairs of samples within each organismal size fraction.
source: K-mers of 31 base pairs (bp) derived from the first 100 million reads sequenced in each sample (or the first 30 million reads for the 0–0.2 µm size fraction) were used to compute a similarity measure between all pairs of samples within each organismal size fraction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the computational method.

claim: 100 million reads per sample were selected because increasing this number did not produce a qualitatively different set of results.
source: Based on a benchmark of Simka, we selected 100 million reads per sample (or 30 million for the 0–0.2 µm fraction) because increasing this number did not produce a qualitatively different set of results, and to ensure that the same number of reads was used in each pairwise comparison within a size fraction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly justifies the choice of read number.

claim: Nearly all samples in the data set had at least 100 million reads (or at least 30 million for the 0–0.2 µm fraction).
source: Nearly all samples in our data set had at least 100 million reads (or at least 30 million for the 0–0.2 µm fraction; Supplementary Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the data availability with reference to a supplementary table.

claim: UPGMA clustering has been shown to have the best performance to describe clustering of regions for organismal biogeography (Kreft and Jetz, 2010).
source: We used UPGMA (unweighted pair-group method using arithmetic averages) clustering, as it has been shown to have the best performance to describe clustering of regions for organismal biogeography (Kreft and Jetz, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly justifies the choice of clustering method with a supporting citation.

claim: The MITgcm Darwin simulation is based on an optimized global ocean circulation model from the ECCO2 group (Menemenlis et al., 2008).
source: We derived travel times from the MITgcm Darwin simulation (Clayton et al., 2016) based on an optimized global ocean circulation model from the ECCO2 group (Menemenlis et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the model with supporting citations.

claim: The horizontal resolution of the MITgcm model was approximately 18 km.
source: The horizontal resolution of the model was approximately 18 km, with 1,103,735 total ocean cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the model resolution.

claim: The model was run for six continuous years in order to smooth anomalies that might occur during any single year.
source: We ran the model for six continuous years in order to smooth anomalies that might occur during any single year.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly explains the rationale for the model run duration.

claim: A fourth-order Runge-Kutta method with trilinearly interpolated velocities and a diffusion of 100 m²/s was used to simulate transport.
source: We used a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method with trilinearly interpolated velocities and a diffusion of 100 m²/s.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the numerical method.

claim: 1000 trajectories, each 10,000 years long, were constructed for each float released within a 200 km radius of a Tara station.
source: Second, following previous studies (Hellweger et al., 2014), we stitched together monthly trajectories to create 10,000-year trajectories: for each float released within a 200 km radius of a Tara station, we constructed 1000 trajectories, each 10,000 years long.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the trajectory construction with a supporting citation.

claim: 50.8 million trajectories were generated in total.
source: We searched the resulting 50.8 million trajectories for those that connected pairs of Tara Oceans stations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of trajectories.

claim: Only pairs of stations connected by more than 1000 trajectories were included to ensure robustness of results.
source: To ensure robustness of our results, we only included pairs of stations that were connected by more than 1000 trajectories.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the inclusion criterion.

claim: Correlation analyses were restricted to Tara Oceans samples collected at the surface and did not include DCM samples.
source: Our correlation analyses were restricted to Tara Oceans samples collected at the surface and did not include DCM samples.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the scope of correlation analyses.

claim: Stations that were not from open ocean locations were excluded from correlation analyses to avoid sites impacted by coastal processes.
source: We excluded stations that were not from open ocean locations from correlation analyses to avoid sites impacted by coastal processes (those numbered 54, 61, 62, 79, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120, and 121).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the exclusion criterion with specific station numbers.

claim: Rank-based Spearman correlations were calculated with a Mantel test with 1000 permutations and a nominal significance threshold of p<0.01.
source: We calculated rank-based Spearman correlations between β-diversity, Tmin, and environmental parameters (either differences in temperature or the Euclidean distance composed of differences in NO3 + NO2, PO4, and Fe, see above) for surface samples with a Mantel test with 1000 permutations and a nominal significance threshold of p<0.01.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the statistical method.

claim: Tara Oceans samples within the subtropical gyre of the North Atlantic and in the Mediterranean Sea were all collected in winter.
source: As the Tara Oceans samples within the subtropical gyre of the North Atlantic and in the Mediterranean Sea were all collected in winter, seasonal variations should not play a role in the variability in community composition that we observed (see Supplementary Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sampling season with reference to a supplementary table.

claim: Genomic e-folding times were calculated based on an exponential fit of metagenomic dissimilarity to Tmin with the form y = C0 e−x/τ.
source: We calculated genomic e-folding times (the time after which the detected genomic similarity between plankton communities changes by 63%) over scales from months to years based on an exponential fit of metagenomic dissimilarity to Tmin with the form y = C0 e−x/τ (where C0 is a constant and τ is the folding time).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the calculation method.

claim: Exponential fits for size fractions 0–0.2 µm and 5–20 µm were not calculated due to an insufficient number of sampled stations in the North Atlantic.
source: Exponential fits for size fractions 0–0.2 µm and 5–20 µm were not calculated due to an insufficient number of sampled stations in the North Atlantic (Appendix 6).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this limitation with reference to an appendix.

claim: Plankton were collected using WP2 (200 µm mesh) nets, using vertical tows (0–100 m), and preserved with borax-buffered formaldehyde.
source: Plankton were also collected using WP2 (200 µm mesh) nets, using vertical tows (0–100 m), and preserved with borax-buffered formaldehyde.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the imaging sample collection method.

claim: All genomic data were collected during day time.
source: Since all genomic data were collected during day time, we restricted our analysis on day-collected samples.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timing of genomic data collection.

claim: MAG relative abundances in metagenomic samples were retrieved from Delmont et al., 2022a.
source: MAG relative abundances in metagenomic samples were retrieved from Delmont et al., 2022a.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly cites the source of MAG data.

claim: β-diversity was estimated by calculating the Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between pairs of stations based on the relative abundances of each of the 713 MAGs.
source: β-diversity was estimated by calculating the Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between pairs of stations based on the relative abundances of each of the 713 MAGs calculated by read mapping in the metagenomes of size fraction 20–180 µm (the size fraction in which MAGs recruit the largest relative share of all reads).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MAG-based β-diversity calculation.

claim: For each sample, the average percentage of prokaryote or eukaryote reads represents the average across all samples within a given size fraction.
source: For the remaining 538 samples, the average percentage represents the average across all samples within a given size fraction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes how the average percentages were calculated.

claim: Samples for which both prokaryote and eukaryote relative counts had a zero or negligible sum (<1% of total reads) were discarded.
source: We discarded samples for which both prokaryote and eukaryote relative counts had a zero or negligible sum (<1% of total reads).
